title: CONSUMABLE SALES
content:
Consumables are attractive for an obvious reason: customers use them up. If the product works for them, they may need it again and again.

But there is an important difference between a product that gets purchased repeatedly and a seller who gets paid repeatedly.

Imagine someone clicks your affiliate link and buys a package of Oreos. Eventually, the Oreos are gone. The customer buys more, but this time they grab them at a grocery store. The product created repeat demand, but that repeat purchase did not create repeat income for you.

Other structures can work differently. A customer account might remain connected to a particular seller, or the customer may intentionally return to the same store or brand. The actual economics depend on what happens when the customer needs the product again.

REPEAT DEMAND IS VALUABLE, BUT WHO CAPTURES IT?
A customer might love a skincare product and buy it every six weeks. Whether that creates repeat business for you depends on how the next order happens. Your own brand, your store, an attributed customer account, and a one-time affiliate link can all produce different outcomes.

AUTOSHIP DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT THE CUSTOMER VALUES
If another bag of dog food ships every month, the recurring schedule is a convenient replenishment mechanism. The underlying value is still the dog food being used up. Later, the subscription branch will focus on continued payment for continued access or value.

REORDER MAP
For any consumable idea, write:
FIRST PURCHASE: How does the customer buy from or through me?
PRODUCT RUNS OUT: Approximately what happens next?
REORDER: What action must the customer take?
ATTRIBUTION: What makes that order mine?
COMPENSATION: Exactly why do I get paid again?

If you cannot answer the last two yet, you have found the next thing to research.

The central question for this entire branch is:
WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE CUSTOMER NEEDS IT AGAIN?

If a business built around products people use up sounds appealing → PDF 21.
If not → PDF 02.

WHY THIS QUESTION COMES SO EARLY
If repeat purchasing is the main reason a consumable model appeals to you, you need to know whether YOUR business actually benefits from that repetition before choosing the method of selling it. Otherwise, you can accidentally select a repeat-purchase product while building one-off economics for yourself.

REPEAT DEMAND IS ONLY HALF OF THE EQUATION

Consumables are attractive because the customer's need can naturally return. Shampoo runs out. Coffee gets consumed. Pet food gets eaten. Supplements get used. Cleaning products need replacing. That creates the possibility of repeat purchasing without requiring you to invent an entirely new reason for the customer to buy.

But the repeat demand belongs to the PRODUCT CATEGORY. It does not automatically belong to YOU.

Imagine that you recommend a package of Oreos through an affiliate link. The customer buys once, likes the product, and later buys Oreos at a grocery store. The product had repeat demand, but your business captured only the first transaction.

Now imagine a customer account that remains attributed to a particular seller and pays that seller on future qualifying orders. The underlying product may be equally consumable, but the seller's repeat economics are different because the customer relationship and compensation rules persist.

A third version is your own branded consumable. If customers reorder directly from your business, you may capture the repeat purchase, but now you also carry the responsibilities that come with owning the product and customer relationship.

AUTOSHIP DOES NOT CHANGE THE CATEGORY

Automatic replenishment can make repeat ordering easier, but a bag of coffee shipped every month is still a consumable if the reason for the next shipment is that the coffee gets used up. The customer is paying for another unit of product, not for continued access to an ongoing service or experience.

This distinction matters later when you compare consumables with subscriptions. Similar billing schedules can hide very different businesses.

THE REORDER TEST

For any consumable idea, trace the customer through at least three purchases.

Purchase one: How do they buy, and how do you get paid?

Purchase two: What causes them to return, where do they place the order, and are you still connected to it?

Purchase ten: If they become a loyal customer, what relationship still exists between them, the product source, and your business?

If you cannot explain that path yet, that is not a failure. It tells you exactly what needs to be investigated before repeat purchasing becomes part of your business case.

FOLLOW THE SAME CUSTOMER FOR A YEAR

Consider a customer who buys a $40 consumable every month.

MODEL A: ORDINARY AFFILIATE REFERRAL
In January, the customer clicks your link and buys from the merchant. Assume the program credits that purchase to you. In February, the customer remembers the product name and buys it directly from the merchant, through an app, at a store, or through somebody else's link. Unless the program has a mechanism that continues connecting that customer to you, February's purchase may create nothing for your business.

The customer can remain a perfect repeat PRODUCT customer while becoming a one-time customer from your economic perspective.

MODEL B: YOUR OWN PRODUCT
The customer buys your branded $40 product from your store in January. When it runs out, they return to your store in February and buy another. You capture the second retail sale because the product and customer transaction are yours.

That does not make the revenue automatic. The customer can switch brands, forget to reorder, dislike the product, or buy an alternative. You still have to earn retention. But there is a direct path for a loyal customer to purchase from you repeatedly.

MODEL C: PERSISTENT CUSTOMER ATTRIBUTION
The customer creates an account through a selling arrangement that associates them with you. If the current compensation rules say their qualifying future purchases continue generating compensation for you, their February order can create another payment even though another company owns and fulfills the product.

Now the repeat economics come from the compensation and attribution structure, not merely from that the item runs out.

WHY THIS DISTINCTION CHANGES THE DECISION

"People need to buy it every month" is not a revenue model. It is a demand characteristic.

To evaluate a consumable business, you need both halves:

1. Why would the customer need or want another unit?
2. What makes that later purchase economically connected to your business?

If you cannot answer the second question, do not count repeat purchases as repeat income yet.

IF YOU LIKE THE IDEA OF REPEAT PURCHASES BUT NOT PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT

That is useful information.

You do not have to own a consumable to build around consumable demand. The existing-product branch lets you explore ways to participate in sales of products another company already makes.

Likewise, if the part that appeals to you is controlling the product, brand, and retained customer relationship, move toward ownership.

The consumable branch is not asking whether you want to formulate protein powder, make soap, stock coffee, join a direct-selling company, or become an affiliate all at once. Those are later choices.

Right now you are deciding whether a product people naturally use up is the kind of customer behavior you want your business built around.

THE DECISION

The reason to choose consumables is not simply that people can buy them repeatedly. Choose this branch if you like building around replenishment and the possibility of earning repeated purchases from satisfied customers. The next decision is whether the product itself should be yours.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
If the repeat-purchase question interests you, continue to PDF 21. Keep the question "What happens when the customer needs it again?" with you through the entire branch.
